path, so it lands only with the user's approval.

The user's direction: the language of the spec and of any text should be simple and
technical enough for programmers to understand, consistent, and not bloated, without losing
information.

## Goal

**Consistency** (goal 11), applied to the harness's own text: one term per thing, one form
for a condition, a list, a definition. **Maintainability** (goal 6): text a reader can
change without misreading it. No measure of either counts prose yet; the change's own
recurrence signal stands in.

  a figure of its own; what "it", "one", "its" and "those" refer to in four measures; whether

  rules are relaxed and carry the test that every fact stays.
- The standards the rules draw on, not adopted whole: ASD-STE100 (sentence length, one

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
with why. A lesson is not
filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it.

A defect in a tool found while reviewing is such a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed
code, and is filed with its reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- its entry of [Record](#11-record), which the change or its proposal drafts, names a
  recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of
  it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
reviewed with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: recurring lessons are
proposed for the spec, open proposals are landed as the autonomy allows, the working
branches are offered to the user for `devel`, the revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled, and the watched changes
of the record are checked against the module, as an audit checks them at its end.

## 11. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. An entry gives the campaign and proposal the change
came from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence
signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
  passed it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.

## 12. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

1	---
     2	name: authoring
     3	description: "How Crustify itself is organized: skills, roles, tool skills and the plugin, and where each kind of text goes. Read before changing Crustify or writing a task message for an agent."
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Authoring
     7	
     8	How Crustify is organized: its skills, its agents and the providers that serve them to an
     9	agent host, and where each kind of text lives. The aim is that every rule is written once,
    10	in the one place its kind belongs, so that changing it changes every agent that follows it,
    11	and no two copies drift apart.
    12	
    13	## 1. Layers
    14	
    15	Crustify is text in three layers, with one more per run:
    16	
    17	| layer | where | voice | holds |
    18	|---|---|---|---|
    19	| skills | `skills/<group>/<name>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what Crustify's artifacts are and how its work is done: workflows, how-tos, conventions, schemas |
    20	| tool skills | `skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what each tool is, and how it serves each stage |
    21	| agents | `agents/<agent>.md`, with `agents/common.md`, and the assistant's under `agents/assistant/` | instructive, second person | an agent's identity, inputs, what it owns, its steps and what its role changes in the skill index |
    22	| task messages | `task.md` beside a run's `task.json` | instructive | what one run is given: its inputs, and what it needs beyond its role |
    23	
    24	Each artifact's schema, the meaning of its fields, is a skill under `skills/artifacts/`,
    25	and an example of each is given under `templates/`, which the schema cites. The settings,
    26	dashboard and `.gitignore` templates there are what a campaign copies to start. Examples
    27	hold illustrations, not rules.
    28	
    29	The layers are plain Markdown, so that any agent reads them as files. A provider, under
    30	`providers/<host>/`, serves them to one agent host in its own format, as
    31	[Providers](#4-providers) describes; the layers name no host.
    32	
    33	### 1.1 Skills
    34	
    35	A skill describes. It states what an artifact holds, how a decision is made, what a
    36	procedure produces and when each of its steps happens, never what an agent should do, and
    37	never who does a step: which agent owns which step is the agents'. It does not name the
    38	tools that serve it either: a skill reads the same whether or not a tool is installed, so
    39	a statement such as "each unit's lifecycle role is established while planning" belongs in
    40	a skill, and the wavefront command that records it belongs in wavefront's tool skill.
    41	
    42	Skills are grouped by the part of the work they describe: `workflows/`, `planning/`,
    43	`rust/`, `verification/`, `operations/`, `artifacts/`, `tools/` and `crustify/`. A skill's
    44	name is unique across the groups, since agents invoke it by name. Two kinds of skill
    45	describe how work is done. A how-to, such as `binding` or `porting`, describes how one item
    46	is handled. A workflow, under `workflows/`, describes how one kind of campaign proceeds
    47	from its settings to its results: `setup`, which every campaign shares, and one per kind of
    48	campaign (`binding-workflow`, `porting-workflow`, `audit-workflow`). A workflow names the
    49	how-tos and the layout rather than restating them.
    50	
    51	A skill opens with frontmatter that gives its `name` and its `description`. The
    52	description is all an agent sees of the skill before it reads it, so it says what the skill
    53	covers and before which step it is read. A skill stays under about 4,500 tokens, so that a
    54	host that brings an invoked skill back after compacting an agent's context brings it back
    55	whole; one that outgrows that is split at a section that another step needs on its own.
    56	The parts sit in sub-directories of the skill's own, `skills/<group>/<skill>/<part>/SKILL.md`,
    57	each named `<skill>-<part>`, and the skill's own `SKILL.md` keeps what they share: `binding`
    58	and `porting` keep their boundaries, and their `-types` and `-symbols` parts their routes.
    59	
    60	A skill's directory may also hold a script the skill describes, with its tests beside it,
    61	standard library only, so that it runs wherever the skill is read: `usage` holds
    62	`crustify-usage`.
    63	
    64	A skill or an agent says what a step does and which program does it, never the program's
    65	command lines, flags or options, which change with the program: the program's own `--help`
    66	and documentation give them, and the text sends its reader there. A command appears only
    67	where its exact form is what must hold, and a procedure of several commands that must run
    68	exactly so is a script beside its skill, documented by its own `--help`.
    69	
    70	Every skill's sections are numbered. A reference to a section names it, with or without its
    71	number ("testing-builds' Coverage section", "layout § Lifecycle › Waves"), so that a renumbering
    72	never silently points a reference at another section. A skill links another by its
    73	relative path, with the other's name as the link's text.
    74	
    75	### 1.2 Agents
    76	
    77	An agent instructs. Its file holds what is specific to it: its place among the agents, its
    78	inputs, its workflow steps, and the guidelines that apply to one step or stage. Where a step
    79	follows a skill, the agent names the skill's section rather than restating it ("as the
    80	`scheduling` skill's Order section describes"); where a step adds to it, the agent states
    81	only the addition.
    82	
    83	An agent states what it owns by naming the skill sections it carries out ("you create and
    84	purge every level of the `layout` skill's Lifecycle section"), and adds only what the
    85	skills leave to it: the commands it runs, the judgements it makes, the cases it must not
    86	handle itself.
    87	
    88	Every agent's prompt opens with `agents/common.md`: that every commit takes the identity
    89	[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives, that a task
    90	message's instructions take precedence over the rest of the prompt, except where a skill or a
    91	role says a task message adds to a check and never relaxes it, and how skills and
    92	tool skills are read. Every agent sees every skill, with its description:
    93	its host lists them, or, for a host that does not, the provider fills the index of every
    94	skill at common's `<!-- SKILL INDEX -->` marker from the skills' names and descriptions, so
    95	that each description is written once.
    96	
    97	The agent's own file follows, in three sections, every agent alike:
    98	
    99	- `## Role`: who the agent is, its place among the agents, what it owns and what it leaves
   100	  to others;
   101	- `## Workflow`: its steps, each naming the skills it follows. A skill the description
   102	  already sends the agent to before a step needs no mention; a step names a skill where
   103	  only part of it applies to the agent, or where the agent follows it only in some runs;
   104	  and
   105	- `## Inputs`: what its task message names.
   106	
   107	An agent's file names no value of one run: an integration branch or a batch id is "the one
   108	your task message names". `{crustify_root}` stands for the path of Crustify's checkout,
   109	which a provider fills.
   110	
   111	The assistant has one file for every kind of campaign, `agents/assistant/assistant.md`, with a
   112	`<!-- CAMPAIGN ROLE -->` marker at the end of its Role and a `<!-- CAMPAIGN WORKFLOW -->`
   113	marker as its Workflow, which take the campaign kind's file,
   114	`agents/assistant/translate.md` for a port or wrap campaign or `agents/assistant/audit.md`
   115	for an audit: its `### Campaign` section, what the assistant owns in that kind of campaign,
   116	and, after its `<!-- WORKFLOW -->` marker, its steps.
   117	
   118	### 1.3 Tool skills
   119	
   120	A tool is one program an agent reaches for: wavefront, ffimap, ffibox. Each has one skill,
   121	`skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md`, written as every skill is, descriptively and without naming
   122	agents. It states what a campaign uses the tool for, where the tool's state sits in a
   123	campaign, and how the tool's output becomes Crustify's artifacts and decisions. How the
   124	tool works, its configuration, tables, commands and what they mean, is its own
   125	documentation's, which the skill cites by document rather than restating, so that the two
   126	never drift; a fact that documentation lacks is added to it, on a branch of the tool's
   127	repository, not to the skill.
   128	
   129	A tool skill opens with what the tool is, which documentation of its own is read in full
   130	before its first use, and what holds in every use of it; one section per stage follows,
   131	each subsection named after the skill section it adds to ("Scheduling › Order"), stating
   132	only what the tool adds there and naming the documents of the tool that stage reads. Its
   133	description names the stages and steps it serves.
   134	
   135	An agent reads a tool's skill before the first step of its work that the skill's
   136	description names, as `agents/common.md` says, and no other skill names a tool: the
   137	description alone brings an agent to the tool, so it names every stage and step the tool
   138	serves. A tool is removed by deleting its skill.
   139	
   140	## 2. Placement
   141	
   142	| text | goes in |
   143	|---|---|
   144	| what an artifact's fields mean | its schema skill under `skills/artifacts/` |
   145	| what an artifact looks like | its example under `templates/` |
   146	| how a kind of work is done, independent of tools | the skill for that work |
   147	| how a kind of campaign proceeds, step by step | its workflow skill under `skills/workflows/`, with the steps every campaign shares in `setup` |
   148	| a convention every agent follows | `conventions` |
   149	| what one agent does, in which steps, and which steps it owns | that agent's file under `agents/` |
   150	| what every agent holds | `agents/common.md` |
   151	| what the assistant does in one kind of campaign | `agents/assistant/<kind>.md` |
   152	| what a tool is, and how it serves each stage | its tool skill |
   153	| how one host is served the layers | its provider under `providers/<host>/` |
   154	| what one run needs beyond its role | its task message, `task.md` |
   155	| what Crustify is for, which every change is judged against | `GOALS.md`, at Crustify's root |
   156	| how Crustify repairs and improves itself | [`evolution`](../evolution/SKILL.md) |
   157	| which changes landed, and whether each held | `EVOLUTION.md`, at Crustify's root |
   158	| a rule that holds for one target alone | that campaign's `crustify/LESSONS.md` |
   159	
   160	A rule that two agents share goes in a skill both read, not in both agents. A rule that
   161	names a tool goes in the tool's skill. A change to a rule is made where the rule lives;
   162	text that restates it elsewhere is removed rather than kept in step.
   163	
   164	## 3. Runs
   165	
   166	A stage's agent runs with its file as its system prompt and its task as its first message:
   167	the task message names what its `## Inputs` section lists and the instructions its run
   168	needs beyond its role, if any. Its file is the same for every run of the stage, so that runs at once share their
   169	whole system prompt in the provider's cache. The assistant runs the same way, as the main
   170	agent of a session in a campaign's repository, with its file and its campaign kind's as
   171	its system prompt.
   172	
   173	## 4. Providers
   174	
   175	A provider serves the layers to one agent host, in that host's format, and holds nothing
   176	the layers do not: every file it carries is generated from them, wires them in, or carries
   177	what its host needs of its own.
   178	
   179	The generic provider, `providers/generic/`, composes each agent's prompt for any host:
   180	`compose.py <agent> [<kind>]` prints `agents/common.md`, with the skill index filled, and
   181	the agent's file, the assistant's with its campaign kind's. A host without a provider of
   182	its own takes that prompt as its agent's instructions, and reads each skill's `SKILL.md`
   183	by its path. The other providers compose through it.
   184	
   185	The Claude Code provider, `providers/claude/`, makes Crustify's checkout a plugin, whose
   186	manifest is `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:
   187	
   188	- the skills, by their group directories and the directory of each part of a split skill,
   189	  which the manifest lists on its own since Claude Code scans a listed directory one level
   190	  deep, invoked as `crustify:<name>`;
   191	- `agents/`, one plugin agent per stage, `crustify:<stage>`, and one assistant per campaign
   192	  kind, `crustify:assistant-translate` and `crustify:assistant-audit`. A plugin agent's
   193	  body replaces Claude Code's own system prompt, so each body opens with that prompt,
   194	  `system-prompt.md`, followed by the generic provider's prompt without the skill index,
   195	  since Claude Code lists the plugin's skills to every agent. Each agent's
   196	  frontmatter gives the description the assistant routes a run by;
   197	- `system-prompt.md`, Claude Code's own system prompt, captured from a real request by
   198	  `dump-system-prompt.py`, less its one project's `# Memory` section, and dumped again
   199	  when Claude Code is upgraded;
   200	- `spawn.py`, which launches a stage run as a Claude Code process of its own, since Claude
   201	  Code refuses a subagent's writes of report files, and copies its transcript into
   202	  Crustify's home; the assistants' prompts end with how they launch through it;
   203	- `hooks.json`: a `SubagentStop` hook, `transcripts.py`, which copies each stage agent's
   204	  transcript into Crustify's home, for a stage run a host launches as a subagent; and
   205	- `compose.py`, which generates the agents (`compose.py build`).
   206	
   207	The generated files are committed, and regenerated whenever `agents/` or
   208	`system-prompt.md` changes.
   209	
   210	## 5. Language

    78	inputs, its workflow steps, and the guidelines that apply to one step or stage. Where a step
    79	follows a skill, the agent names the skill's section rather than restating it ("as the

    81	only the addition.

   102	  already sends the agent to before a step needs no mention; a step names a skill where

Review is tiered. Each landing is reviewed within its wave, to the depth
[Depth](#11-depth) gives it. Before a module's switch in a port, and at its end in a
wrap, a module pass reviews the module whole, across its batches: its unsafe regions, its
exports and its tests. It is the last review batch of the last wave of the module's `wrap`
and `port` items, not of a port's later stages, marked
`module_pass`, launched once every other batch of that wave has landed; its worklist is
the module's paths, and it runs the wave's gates and the module's end gates, as
[Gates](#7-gates) describes. A module whose run landed a single translation batch is
reviewed by its module pass alone, whose workset is that batch's whole: a review of the
batch before it would read the same code twice.

Review batches are packed eagerly, as the batches they review land: one launches as soon as
the landed batches not yet reviewed fill it, and the last once every translation batch of
the wave has landed, so that review runs beside the wave's remaining batches rather than
after them. When a session runs only part of a wave, or part of the scope, its review
covers what it landed, before what consumes that starts.

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), before planning an audit's worksets, and when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

**Verdict: rejected.** Seven fixes are needed, all small. Nothing is lost: every fact of the old `GOALS.md` is in the new one. The rewrite does break its own firm rules in several places, adds one reading the old text left open, and the `EVOLUTION.md` row misstates a rule. The change weakens no check.

1. **Rule 3 is broken by its own first use.** Five series of three or more phrases stay inline in the new `GOALS.md`:
   - line 82: "by a review, at a switch, or by a consumer"
   - line 106: "batches run again, gates rerun and merges made twice"
   - lines 171–172: "wrapped, ported or moves through its later stages"
   - lines 183–184: "waited for it, rewrote around it or reached past its wrapper"
   - lines 205–206: "worked around, rewrote sound code to satisfy, or reported as forcing…"

   The Language section's own opening also breaks the refinement: it lists "skills; tool skills; agents; …", short names that the refinement says "stay inline". Either bring the text to the rule or reword the rule. I recommend rewording: short names *may* stay inline, and only phrases with clauses of their own must be listed.
2. **Rule 1, used before defined.** "When more escape" (line 28) comes before "escape" is defined (line 31). Move the tier and escape paragraph above the pairing paragraph.
3. **Rule 1, one word for two things.** Line 132's "coverage … by regions" uses "regions", which lines 48 and 55 use for unsafe regions. Use "region coverage", the term `testing-builds` uses (`testing/builds/SKILL.md:75`).
4. **The `EVOLUTION.md` row is wrong in three ways.**
   - It states rule 4 as "within one sentence"; the rule is "the same sentence or the one before".
   - It leaves out both refinements.
   - Its "(this commit)" points only at `73ca306`, the commit that added it.
5. **The `authoring` description is unchanged.** It still says "Read before changing Crustify or writing a task message". The new section covers proposals, but a run that files one only reads `evolution`, so nothing sends it to these rules. The description should name the language rules and proposals.
6. **The scope list falls short of the user's "any text".** It leaves out `LESSONS.md`, `EVOLUTION.md`, templates and review reports. Complete the list, or say it is not exhaustive.
7. **Some readings were settled without being put to the author** (`73ca306`), as the nine were. The one that changes meaning:
   - Line 32, "The later tiers are:", closes a list that the old line 30 left open (examples or the full set).

   These should be confirmed too, though each picks the more likely reading:
   - Soundness's "These defects are…" (line 65)
   - Equivalence's "They are found by…" (line 82)
   - Goal 3's "per item reviewed", now attached to the findings only (line 93)
   - Goal 4's "cheaper work that escapes more…", now attached to the second pair only (lines 107–108)

## 1. Every fact kept

I made my own list of about 65 facts. Each is in the new text:

- **Opening, old lines 3–18 → new lines 3–43:**
  - what Crustify is for, how it evolves, and what every change is judged against (3–4);
  - a rule serving no goal is removed (6);
  - a tension between goals is weighed and stated (6–7);
  - the four evidence kinds (11–14);
  - a change to the goals is proposed under `evolution` and needs the user's approval (16–17);
  - what fitness is, the two sources a measure is read from, and that no run is made only to take it (19–25);
  - pairing, and that neither measure is read alone (27–28);
  - the two examples: fewer findings, cheaper work (28–29);
  - not taken yet means judged, not measured (39–40).
- **Goal 1:**
  - the statement (47–48);
  - the three scan counts (53–55), which two fall (57) and which is zero throughout (58);
  - the pair with soundness and its reason (59–60);
  - the defects, by kind (64–65);
  - the escapes (66);
  - both not-taken items (67–68).
- **Goal 2:** the statement and its definition (72–73), the three measures (76–80), the pair and where differences are found (81–82), the not-taken figures (83–84).
- **Goal 3:** the statement (88–89), the scan forms and the findings (91–93), the pair and its reason (94–95), the not-taken item (96).
- **Goal 4:** the statement (100–101), the harness measure and both pairs (105–108), the emitted-Rust measure and its pair (112–114), not taken (115), the TODO (116–117), kept word for word.
- **Goal 5:** the statement and its means (121–123), the measure (125), both pairs (126–129), the three not-taken items (131–133), the TODO (134).
- **Goal 6:** the statement, word for word (138–140), both reuse measures (142–146), what counts against (148–149), the pair (150–151).
- **Goal 7:** the statement, in three parts (155–157), the measures and the kinds of crossing (159–165), not taken (166). There is no pair, as before.
- **Goal 8:**
  - the statement (170–172), the three measures (175–177), the pair with Idiomatic Rust (178–179);
  - the order's measure (183–184), and the order itself, with the cycle case (186–187);
  - what it says of Safety and Performance (187–188);
  - not taken (189).
- **Goal 9:** the statement (193–194) and both measures (196–198).
- **Goal 10:** the statement, with its condition first (202–203), the measure (205–206), the pair (207–208).
- **Goal 11:**
  - the statement and that a departure states its reason (212–214);
  - the weighing against Least constraint, complete (216–219);
  - the measure, the pair and its reason (221–224), the three not-taken items (226–228).
- **Goal 12:** the statement (232–233), the measure and its two examples (235–237).

What the new text states that the old did not:

- the known definition of a tier (31);
- "Each thing measured is a *measure*" (20) and "which is its *pair*" (28), new terms that add no claim;
- the line describing the document's own layout (42–43);
- the closed list of later tiers (fix 7).

What moved: the definition of an escape left goal 1 (old lines 29–30) for the opening (31), and now covers any defect rather than soundness defects only. That fits the old text's own use of "escape" in its opening (line 16) and in goal 4 (line 52). No fact moved under another goal, and none was weakened.

## 2. The nine settled sentences

The old text allowed all nine of the author's readings.

| # | Settled reading | Another reading at least as likely? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The first two scan counts fall | Yes on the text alone: "which fall" attaches most naturally to the nearest item, as "which is zero throughout" does. `bca1d35`'s "It falls … the last is zero" backs the author's reading. |
| 2 | "The regions" is coverage by regions | No. Goal 1's "regions" made unsafe regions possible, but `ac41d76`'s "by lines and regions" confirms coverage. |
| 3 | Things count against "this measure" | "The goal" was as likely; the meaning is the same either way. |
| 4 | "The target's" lessons | "The campaign's" was as likely; same meaning, and goal 9's own statement says "that target's lesson". |
| 5 | "A rule was loosened" | Yes, syntactically: "a check" is the nearest noun. The two differ in scope, since a rule is broader. The author's reading matches "a loosened rule" at the head of the sentence. |
| 6 | "Those" means both paired measures | "Only the later-tier findings" was possible but not more likely. `ac41d76` already marked reshaped items as not taken. |
| 7 | Attribution's two cases are examples | No. They are a run and a figure, not commits, cells or decisions, so they cannot be a definition of those. |
| 8 | Goal 3's scan is Safety's | No: it is the only scan the text names. |
| 9 | Goal 6's scan is Safety's | No. ffimap's wrapper-use counters (`ffimap/SKILL.md:8-9`) bear it out. |

## 3. The rules against their own text

- **Rule 1:** broken by fixes 2 and 3.
- **Rule 2:** kept, apart from minor edges at lines 157 and 172.
- **Rule 3:** broken (fix 1).
- **Rule 4:** kept.

The defaults are departed from in prose sentences of 28–36 words: lines 138–140, 212–214, 221–224, 94–95 and 178–179. None of these departures keeps information: each splits with nothing lost. Lines 221–224 also join two pairs in one sentence, which is why "both paired measures" (line 226) has no clear referent.

## 4. The two refinements

Both are needed by the text:

- **Rule 2's "only where/when"** is needed by line 131, lines 216–217 and the section's own "Brevity follows only where…".
  - The hole is narrow: "only" turns a condition into a necessary one. Adding it just to keep a condition at the end changes the meaning, and the fact test catches that.
  - The remaining hole is a long trailing restriction. Bound its length.
- **Rule 3's "single words or short names"** is needed by lines 72–73, 88–89, 122–123 and 214.
  - It opens a real hole: "short names" has no bound, and the rewrite used it for the five series in fix 1.
  - "Stays inline" is too strict the other way: the section's own opening list breaks it.

## 5. Placement and consistency

- `authoring` is the right home, and the new section is correctly numbered §5.
- The skill grows from 2,153 to 2,481 words (14,858 characters), roughly 3,300–4,200 tokens. That is under the 4,500 limit, but the margin is thin. No tokenizer is installed here, so this is an estimate.
- No other text of Crustify contradicts the rules. `evolution` §2 ("a change made for style alone … is not made") agrees with the rule that old text is not rewritten wholesale.

## 6. Recurrence signal; weakening

- The row's signal is one a campaign would observe (review verdicts, user corrections), and it is rightly not marked `test`.
- Unless fix 1 is made, this change would meet its own signal at the first check.
- It weakens no check: it adds the fact test, and drops no measure, pair or not-taken marker.

## 7. Build

In a `git archive 01830f8` copy, `python3 -I providers/claude/compose.py build` exited 0, and `git status` over the whole tree was empty afterwards. `providers/claude/` is unchanged.

## What I would word differently (not required)

- "fitness" is defined at line 19 and never used again.
- "count" stands in for "measure" at lines 60 and 178.
- Lists take two forms: capitalised sentences (lines 76–80, 160–177) and lowercase items with semicolons (131–133, 226–228).
- Some entries are fragments starting "Also…" (lines 67, 92, 197).
- Line 133's "its tests" was "the tests" in the old text.
- Line 197 was not reflowed.
- "Never cutting it" sits oddly next to "Brevity follows only where the old text repeated itself"; "never cutting a fact" would fit both.
- "Brings that text to these rules" does not say how far: the sentence, the paragraph, or the section.
- Goal 4's "work that escapes more" uses "escape" as a verb, while the defined term is a noun.

I filed no proposal and recorded no lesson. I did not re-check the subagent's 96-fact checklist, which is not on disk; the fact list above stands in for it.
